notes.short: The ark ahead, the cloud above: one picture
notes.about: Two sentences give one picture: the first names only the ark going ahead to find a resting place, the second only the cloud over the people. Read together, they can show the ark leading the way with the cloud of the LORD above it, guiding and sheltering the march.

lines.words: with the ark of the covenant of the LORD traveling ahead of them for those three days to seek a resting place for them.
And the cloud of the LORD was over them by day when they set out from the camp.

notes.evidence: C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) reads verses 33 and 34 by the laws of poetic parallel lines: one thought, the ark with the cloud above it leading and sheltering the march, is divided into two clauses, the ark alone named in the first and the cloud alone in the second.
notes.limit: Writers differ on where the ark went in the march: in front of the whole camp, or in its middle as the one that led the host.

cites.quote: according to the laws of a poetical parallelism: The one thought that the ark of the covenant, with the cloud soaring above it, led the way and sheltered those who were marching, is divided into two clauses; in Num 10:33 only the ark of the covenant is mentioned as going in front of the Israelites, and in Num 10:34 only the cloud as a shelter over them

notes.about: The spies who brought the bad report say they seemed “like grasshoppers” beside the sons of Anak. By shrinking themselves they make the giants loom larger and the land seem impossible to take. It was the talk of unbelief; Joshua and Caleb answered that the people “will be like bread for us.”

figure.name: Meiosis
figure.words: We seemed like grasshoppers in our own sight
figure.means: the spies' own strength made as small as can be, so that the sons of Anak seem greater still

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Meiosis, the meiosis of unbelief: the spies lessen their own stature to make the sons of Anak seem greater. Benson says fear magnified the giants till the spies felt as contemptible as insects. Jamieson (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it a strong Orientalism in an exaggerated report; Henry hears them as weak and daunted, painting the conquest as impossible.
notes.limit: The note does not deny that the sons of Anak were tall: Moses himself calls them “strong and tall” (Deuteronomy 9:2). The figure lies in how small the spies made themselves.

cites.quote: This is the Meiosis of unbelief. To gain credence for their words they exaggerated the size of the Anakim by lessening their own stature.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Thus their fear magnified these sons of Anak above measure, so that in comparison of them they thought themselves as weak and contemptible as insignificant insects.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: we were in our own sight as grasshoppers--a strong Orientalism, by which the treacherous spies gave an exaggerated report of the physical strength of the people of Canaan.

cites.quote: They represented the conquest of it as altogether impracticable ... But nothing served their ill purpose more than a description of the giants, on whom they lay a great stress ... we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, not only little and weak, but trembling and daunted.

notes.short: The LORD's command, then the deed, in reverse order
notes.about: The command and the deed mirror each other. The LORD speaking to Moses comes first and last; the sentence of death answers the man's death; and at the centre the whole congregation is to stone him outside the camp, and does so.

lines.words: And the LORD said to Moses,
The man must surely be put to death.
The whole congregation is to stone him outside the camp.
So the whole congregation took the man outside the camp and stoned him
as the LORD had commanded Moses.

notes.evidence: E. W. Bullinger lists these verses among introverted parallel lines: the LORD speaking to Moses answers the closing words on His command to Moses, the sentence of death answers the man's dying, the command to stone him answers the stoning, and the congregation outside the camp stands at the centre.

cites.quote: a “And the Lord said unto Moses , b The man shall be surely put to death : c they shall stone him with stones , d all the congregation without the camp. d And they brought him forth, all the congregation without the camp , c and stoned him with stones , b and he died ; a as the Lord commanded Moses.

notes.short: Offerings in the priests' charge are their portion
notes.about: The second clause explains the first. The offerings Aaron is put in charge of are the ones given to him and his sons as a portion, so the priests were to keep the gifts Israel brought as the share that belonged to them.

lines.words: Behold, I have put you in charge of My offerings.
As for all the sacred offerings of the Israelites, I have given them to you and your sons as a portion and a permanent statute.

notes.evidence: C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the notion of keeping in the first clause is defined in the second, parallel clause as a portion: the priests were to keep all the offerings as the portion that belonged to them.
notes.limit: Others take the word rendered portion as anointing: the gifts were the priests' because they had been anointed.

cites.quote: The notion of משׁמרת, keeping, as in Exo 12:6 ; Exo 16:23 , Exo 16:32 , is defined in the second parallel clause as משׁחה, a portion (see at Lev 7:35 ). The priests were to keep all the heave-offerings, as the portion which belonged to them

notes.short: A song people knew, quoted about Heshbon
notes.about: The verse brings in lines from a song people already knew. It follows verses 25 and 26: Israel had taken Heshbon, the city of Sihon, who had won it from the king of Moab.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Quoted as being already in use as such
figure.words: Come to Heshbon, let it be rebuilt; let the city of Sihon be restored
figure.means: a known song on Heshbon, the city Sihon had won from Moab

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Parœmia, among those quoted as being already in use as such, and calls the lines three strophes from a popular poem. Calvin calls it an old saying, well known; Henry, one of the country's proverbs or songs, quoted as proof that the places it names, once Moab's, had become Sihon's; Jamieson (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown), an extract from an Amorite song.
notes.limit: The writers differ on whose song it first was, an Amorite song boasting of conquest or a mocking call to rebuild a city Israel had destroyed, and on whether it ends at verse 28 or verse 30. It is a song of several lines, not a one-line saying.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which are quoted as being already in use as such, p. 756
cites.quote: Parœmiœ which are quoted as being already in use as such ... Three strophes are given from a popular poem, introduced by the word “wherefore.” The first ... is an ironical call to the Amorites to rebuild their city Heshbon, which Israel had destroyed (see verses 25, 26). ... The third (verse 30) is the justification of the woe pronounced in verse 29.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: That is, an old saying, or proverbial sentence remains, and is well known.

For proof of the allegation, he refers to the authentic records of the country, for so their proverbs or songs were, one of which he quotes some passages out of ... which sufficiently proves what is vouched for, namely, [1.] That such and such places that are here named, though they had been in the possession of the Moabites, had by right of war become the dominion of Sihon king of the Amorites.
Here is given an extract from an Amorite song exultingly anticipating an extension of their conquests to Arnon. The quotation from the poem of the Amorite bard ends at Num 21:28.

notes.short: Balak's one demand, said twice in other words
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words. To denounce is to curse, and Jacob is a poet's name for the nation, the same people as Israel. This is what Balak had sent for Balaam to do.

lines.words: put a curse on Jacob for me;

original.note: In Hebrew the verb rendered denounce, za'am, means to be angry; here it is to speak God's wrath, and so the same in sense as curse.

notes.evidence: C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the verb rendered denounce, to be angry and so to utter God's wrath, is synonymous with to curse, and that Jacob is a poetic name for the nation, equivalent to Israel.

cites.quote: "Come, curse me Jacob, and come threaten Israel." Balak had sent for him for this purpose (see Num 22:11 , Num 22:17 ). ... זעם, to be angry, here to give utterance to the wrath of God, synonymous with נקב or קבב, to curse. Jacob: a poetical name for the nation, equivalent to Israel.

notes.short: A people apart, not counted among the nations
notes.about: Read with the second line, dwelling apart means being separate from the other nations, not counted as one of them. Israel did not share their lot, because it had a different God to protect it.

lines.words: not reckoning themselves among the nations.

pairs: not reckoning themselves among the nations
notes.evidence: C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says that, by the parallel clause, dwelling alone means Israel's separation from the rest of the nations: it did not share their lot, having a different God and protector.
notes.limit: Others take dwelling apart as dwelling in safety, undisturbed by other nations.

cites.quote: Dwelling alone does not denote a quiet and safe retirement ... but, according to the parallel clause, "it is not reckoned among the nations," it expresses the separation of Israel from the rest of the nations. ... i.e., it does not share the lot of the other nations, because it has a different God and protector from the heathen

notes.short: A star, a scepter: one ruler to come, named twice
notes.about: The second line says the first again more plainly: the star from Jacob is the scepter from Israel, a ruler still to come. The next two lines pair the same way: crushing Moab is striking down the sons of Sheth, who are read as Moab's own people.

lines.words: A star will come forth from Jacob,
and a scepter will arise from Israel.
He will crush the skulls of Moab
and strike down all the sons of Sheth.

original.note: In Hebrew the rare verb behind strike down, qarqar, is shown to mean destroy by its partner, the verb behind crush.

notes.evidence: John Calvin says the scepter means nothing else than the star, the same thing said twice in the Hebrew way, and that, as Seir explains Edom in the next verse, the sons of Sheth are most likely the Moabites. C. F. Keil: the parallel scepter removes any doubt that the star is a ruler, and the parallel verb fixes the sense destroy. C. J. Elliott (Ellicott): the second symbol clears the first.
notes.limit: The note does not settle whom the ruler is. Some see a first fulfilment in David's victories over Moab and the full one in Christ.

cites.quote: called metaphorically “a Star,” ... for this repetition is common with the Hebrews, by which they particularize the same thing twice over. Assuredly he means nothing else by “the Sceptre,” except what he had indicated by the “Star;” ... Since the form of the two sentences is identical, it is probable that none others than the Moabites are meant by the children of Sheth.

If, however, there could be any doubt that the rising star represented the appearance of a glorious ruler or king, it would be entirely removed by the parallel, "a sceptre arises out of Israel." ... the meaning to destroy is fully established by the parallel מחץ ... by which, according to the analogy of Jacob and Israel ( Num 24:17 ), Edom and Seir ( Num 24:18 ), the Moabites are to be understood

cites.quote: If there is any ambiguity in the first symbol it is removed in the second. A star is a fitting image of an illustrious king or ruler, and the mention of the sceptre in the words which follow (comp. Gen 49:10 ) shows that it is so employed in the present instance.
